Image retrieval, drawn

Q2 is one idea used four times. Turn each image into a vector φ(x), measure a distance d(φ(q), φ(xj)) to every database image, and return the index of the smallest. The four modes differ only in what φ keeps and what it throws away, which is exactly what 2c asks you to explain. Everything below is computed live in your browser from your six images.

1 · the idea

Retrieval is a 1-nearest-neighbour search in feature space

The same rule as kNN with k = 1 W1 §1.3: store the database, compute a distance from the query to each entry, return the closest. The features decide what “close” means W1 §1.2: “The choice of φ determines which relationships a simple model can express.” Pick a mode and a metric below and watch the answer change.

feature φ
metric d

Distances are only comparable within one row of the picture: pixel L2 is in intensity units, χ² is dimensionless, VGG L2 is in activation units. Never compare a pixel distance with a VGG distance.

2 · mode 1 · raw pixels

One long vector, compared entry by entry

φ(x) = vec(I) with d = H·W·C = 224·224·3 = 150,528 numbers W1 §1.2. The distance is the Euclidean one W1 §1.3, which is also the sum of squared errors from Q1 W1 §3.1, now between two images instead of a prediction and a target. Nothing in this vector knows that pixel (10, 10) and pixel (10, 11) are neighbours.

3 · mode 2 · colour histogram

Count how much of each intensity there is, forget where it is

For each channel c, put every pixel value v ∈ [0,1] into one of B bins, bin = min(⌊B·v⌋, B−1) (your clamp handles v = 1), then divide the counts by H·W. Each channel's histogram is now non-negative and sums to 1, a probability vector like the ones in W1 §2.2. φ has 3·B = 192 numbers for B = 64. Two histograms are compared with χ², Σ (p − q)² / (p + q + 10⁻¹⁰): a symmetric distance (KL is not W1 §2.2) that never divides by zero.

4 · mode 3 · VGG19 features

A pretrained network turns 150,528 pixel values into 25,088 feature values

VGG19's vgg.features is a stack of 3×3 convolutions with ReLU, and five 2×2 max-pools W4 §3.1 W4 §4.2 W5 §5.1.5. What comes out is a tensor of shape 512 × 7 × 7, flattened to one vector. Four steps: the shapes, one convolution by hand, what each depth looks like, then the distance itself.

4a · shapes and receptive fields

Each pool halves the grid: 224 → 112 → 56 → 28 → 14 → 7, since 224 / 2⁵ = 7. The vector φ(x) has 7·7·512 = 25,088 entries. The receptive field recursion rℓ = rℓ−1 + (kℓ − 1)·jℓ−1, jℓ = sℓ·jℓ−1 W5 §5.1.4 gives 268 pixels at pool5, which is larger than the 224-pixel input: in theory each of the 49 cells can see the whole image, so the 7×7 grid is not a clean cut-up of the picture (the notes add that the real influence is not uniform).

4b · one convolution, by hand

The first layer has 64 filters of size 3×3×3. Each output pixel is y[i,j] = b + Σc Σm Σn wc[m,n] · xc[i+m, j+n], then ReLU W4 Eq. 3 W4 Eq. 7. Your notes' Eq. 2 divides by Σw to build a weighted average; a learned layer has no such normaliser, it just learns w and b W4 §4.1. Pick a filter, then move over the picture to see one output pixel computed.

Each swatch shows one filter's 3×3 RGB weights, normalised per filter for display only W5 §5.10.2.

input224×224
ReLU(conv)this filter

The input to the real network is the image minus the training-set mean colour, zero-padded by one pixel at the border, so the “zero” the filter sees is a mean-grey pixel. The output map is scaled to its own maximum, which hides magnitudes between filters W5 §5.10.2.

4c · what each depth keeps

Mean over all channels of the activations after each pool, one shared brightness scale per column so strengths stay comparable W5 §5.10.3. Early maps are close to the picture, later ones are small, coarse and image-specific. Look at the last column and at the norm printed under each name.

4d · the 25,088 numbers and their distance

The last step flattens pool5 and takes the L2 distance, so the sum runs over all 49 cells × 512 channels: d² = Σc Σp (Fq[c,p] − Fx[c,p])². Left: one channel's 7×7 map for each image (the channel is only a pattern the network learned, not a named detector W5 §5.10.3). Right: where on the grid the distance comes from.

5 · mode 4 · Gram matrix of the VGG features

Which features fire together, summed over where

Reshape the pool5 tensor to a matrix F with 512 rows (channels) and 49 columns (positions). Then G = F Fᵀ / (C·H·W), a 512×512 matrix. Its entry Gij = Σp F[i,p]·F[j,p] / 25,088 is the dot product of channel i's map with channel j's map: large when the two patterns are active in the same places. The sum over p throws the positions away. Set X = Fᵀ (49 rows, 512 columns) and G is XᵀX, the same Gram matrix that appears in Q1's normal equation W1 §3.1. Your distance is the Frobenius norm of Gq − Gx, the L2 norm of the flattened difference.

7 · question 2b

Choosing one method for a hidden query and database

The hidden images are between 64×64 and 256×256, and you must return an index plus a distance list from one function. I will not pick your method; here is the evidence to pick with. Each database image was edited and used as a query: a feature passes if the edited copy still finds its own original among the five. Mirror, darker (×0.6) and crop 60% are the three edits in your notebook's test cell; shift (40, 25) px is mine.

Each square is one database image (tabby, dog, goldfish, rose, horse, in order). Green = found its own original; red = retrieved another one (its first letter). Hover a square for the distance to its original against the best wrong one.

What the size range does to each feature

pixelsLength depends on H·W, so two sizes cannot be subtracted. You must resize to one fixed size first; the resize itself changes pixel values.
histogramDivided by H·W, so any size gives 3·B numbers that are directly comparable. No resize needed, but the image statistics still shift when you resize.
VGG19 featuresThe convolutions accept any size ≥ 32 px, but the flattened length is 512·(H/32)·(W/32), so different sizes cannot be subtracted. Resize, as the preprocessing already does.
GramAlways 512×512, and divided by C·H·W, so any size gives comparable matrices without resizing. Cost: a 262,144-number vector per image, half of it redundant (G is symmetric).

Things worth testing before you commit

  1. Normalise. Section 6 shows the winner flipping with the metric, and the table above shows plain-L2 VGG failing on every shifted image. Check the feature norms in your own notebook: [float(np.linalg.norm(np.asarray(f).ravel())) for f in feats]. If one image has a much smaller norm, L2 will keep calling it the nearest.
  2. Say what the hidden query probably varies. Colour palette, layout, texture, object? Q4g in this same notebook asks how to use Section 4's answer to build a good hidden test image for Q2, so read it before choosing.
  3. Test your own edits with the harness in the notebook, not only the three given: shift, scale, rotation, a different object on the same background. A method you can describe the failures of is easier to defend in 2c.
  4. Return types. index must be a plain int and distance_list a list of Python floats (.tolist()), or your own test cell flags it.
